video_caption: The video opens with a first-person perspective within a video game, showing two hands, one with a silver ring on the ring finger, seemingly casting a spell or emitting light. In the background, a vibrant, mountainous landscape with evergreen trees and a body of water is visible under a clear blue sky. Overlaid on the screen are the words "BREAK UP TILING IN UNREAL", with two yellow rectangular boxes highlighting areas of repeated texture patterns on a distant hill and closer to the water, visually demonstrating the "tiling" issue the text refers to. The game's user interface is subtly visible at the top center.

The video segment begins by showcasing a green textured plane in Unreal Engine, labeled "Bad Texture," where distinct seams are visible across its surface, highlighted by the accompanying "BadGrassMaterial" in the Content Browser. The user then opens the "BadGrassMaterial" editor, revealing a simple material graph with a "Texture Sample" (displaying the seamed grass texture) connected to "Base Color" and a "Constant" node set to 0.5 connected to "Roughness." To demonstrate a seamless texture, the user navigates to Google Images, searches for "grass texture," then proceeds to the Quixel Megascans website, searches for "wild grass," and downloads a "Wild Grass" material, observing its seamless preview. Back in Unreal Engine, the user imports the downloaded "WildGrass" textures (Albedo, Displacement, Normal) into a new folder named "WildGrassTextures" within the Content Browser, creates a new material called "M_WildGrass," and configures its material graph. This new graph connects the "WildGrass_AO_Albedo" texture to "Base Color," the "WildGrass_AO_Normal" texture to "Normal," and a "Constant" node (value 0.5) to "Roughness," as seen on the preview sphere. After saving the "M_WildGrass" asset, the Unreal Engine level is updated to display two planes: the original "Bad Texture" on the left with its noticeable seams, and a new "Seamless Texture" plane on the right, now flawlessly covered with the newly created "M_WildGrass" material.

The video opens with a split screen within an Unreal Engine editor, showcasing two large, textured planes on a dark blue background. The left plane is labeled "Bad Texture," displaying a distinctly tiled green texture, while the right plane, labeled "Seamless Texture," shows a uniformly textured green surface. Below, the "Content Browser" displays folders and a material sphere labeled "M_GrassMicroVariation." The scene transitions to the Unreal Engine Material Graph editor. On the left, a spherical preview object displays a green, textured surface, rotating slowly. The main graph area shows several interconnected nodes, including two "Texture Sample" nodes. The speaker adds a "TexCoord" (Texture Coordinate) node and then a "Scalar Parameter" node, which is named "MicroTiling." He then adds a "Multiply" node and connects the "Texture Coordinate" node to one input of the "Multiply" node and the "MicroTiling" parameter to the other. Finally, the output of the "Multiply" node is connected to the UV input of the top "Texture Sample" node, and the preview sphere's texture briefly shifts as these connections are made.

The video displays a computer screen showing the Unreal Engine interface for a material graph named "M_GrassMicroVariation." On the left, a spherical object textured with green grass is visible in a preview window, with a "Details" panel open below it. The main part of the screen shows a node-based material editor. A user's cursor is active within the graph, typing "vector" into a search bar to create a new "VectorParameter" node, which currently has a black default color. This new node is intended to be multiplied with the output of a "TextureSample" node (showing a green grass texture) to create a tint, and the result is connected to the "Base Color" input of the "Material Output" node. Below this sequence, another "TextureSample" node with a blue texture is connected to the "Normal" input.

The video displays a screen recording of the Unreal Engine material editor. On the left, a preview pane shows a spherical object with a green, moss-like texture, labeled "M_GrassMicroVariation." The main area of the screen shows a material graph with interconnected nodes. A person, whose hands are not visible, is demonstrating how to modify the material. At 0:06, a search bar pops up, and the person types "Texture Sample" to create a new node. They then select "T_MacroVariation" from a dropdown list of textures, which is added to the graph at 0:13. Next, they create a "Texture Coordinate" node at 0:19 and connect its output to the 'UVs' input of a "Multiply" node. They then create a "Scalar Parameter" at 0:22, naming it "MacroVariationAlphaTiling," and connect this parameter to the 'B' input of the "Multiply" node, which is then connected to the 'UVs' input of the "Texture Sample" node. At 0:28, the value of the "MacroVariationAlphaTiling" parameter is set to "0.01." Finally, at 0:31, a "Linear Interpolate" node is created and placed in the graph.

The video segment opens in the Unreal Engine Material Graph editor, where a user connects the output of a "Lerp" (LinearInterpolate) node to the "Base Color" input of the main "Material Output" node, demonstrating how color variations are blended. A preview sphere on the left displays a green, grass-like material. The screen then transitions to the Unreal Engine Level Editor, showing two flat planes labeled "Bad Textures" on the left, displaying a highly repetitive green texture, and "Seamless Texture" on the right. The user applies the "M_GrassMicroVariation" material to the right plane, causing its texture to change from a uniform green to a more varied, less repetitive grass, which is then labeled "MicroVariation". A tooltip displays details of the applied material. Subsequently, a "Color Picker" window appears, allowing the user to interactively adjust the material's color from a yellowish-green to a richer green, with the changes reflected instantly on the grass texture in the level and on a preview sphere within the color picker. The "Details" panel on the right also shows various material parameters.

The video displays a split-screen view within a software environment, likely a game engine, showcasing different grass textures on three flat planes. From left to right, these planes are labeled "Bad Texture," showing a visibly tiled green texture, "Seamless Texture," displaying a uniformly green texture, and "MicroVariation," presenting a green texture with subtle, less repetitive patterns. The user's cursor is active within the software, and a "Content Browser" in the bottom left shows two material icons, one lighter green and one darker green, labeled "M_MacroVariationNoise" and "M_Test_GrassVariation" respectively, with "M_MacroVariationNoise" highlighted. An "Outliner" panel on the right lists several "Floor" actors, indicating different planes or objects in the scene.

The video displays the Unreal Engine 5 interface with a dark theme. In the main viewport, a 3D landscape is visible, featuring undulating green terrain in the foreground and a flat, grey area in the distance, all under a dark blue sky. The camera subtly pans across this landscape. On the right, the "Outliner" panel lists scene elements like "Lighting," "SM_SkySphere," and "Landscape." Below the main viewport, the "Content Browser" shows a selected folder named "MacroDistanceBlend," containing a material asset titled "M_MacroDistanceBlend," depicted by a spherical preview of a mottled green texture. At 0:08, hovering over this asset reveals a tooltip with its details, including "NAME: M_MacroDistanceBlend," "PATH: /Game/Content/MacroDistanceBlend/M_MacroDistanceBlend," "CLASS: Material," and other properties like "CASTS SHADOWS: True." A male voice narrates, discussing how, despite added variation, textures can still appear tiled in large environments when viewed from a distance, directly correlating with the visual content of working with landscape materials in a game engine.

The video begins with a view of the Unreal Engine editor, displaying a landscape composed of green terrain and a grey/black section, along with a floating "M_MacroDistanceBlend Material" popup window detailing its asset type and disk size. The scene transitions to the Material Graph editor, where the narrator explains the process of setting up distance-based material blending. He selects a group of nodes labeled "MacroColor," "MacroColorVariation," and "MacroVariationBlend," places them within a comment box named "Near," and then duplicates this entire group, naming the new comment box "Far." Within the "Far" group, he renames and adjusts scalar parameters: "FarTiling" is set to 0.05, "FarVariationTiling" to 0.05, and a newly created "FarVariationAlphaTiling" is set to 0.001, while also renaming tint parameters to "FarTint" and "FarVariationTint." To control the blending, he creates a "PixelDepth" node, subtracts a "FarDistance" scalar (defaulting to 5000) from it, divides the result by a "FarFadeAmount" scalar (defaulting to 7500), and then clamps the output between 0 and 1. These nodes are grouped into a comment titled "Create Gradient From Camera." Finally, this clamped output is connected to the alpha input of a "Lerp" node that combines the "Near" and "Far" material groups. The material is then applied to the landscape in the main editor, demonstrating a smooth transition from the detailed green "Near" texture up close to a simpler white/gray "Far" texture in the distance.

The video demonstrates how to create a distance-based material blend in Unreal Engine. It starts by showing a landscape with a shader that displays black close to the camera and white further away, with a smooth gradient in between, indicating where near and far textures will eventually be applied. The scene then transitions to the Material Graph editor for "M_MacroDistanceBlend," where the user manipulates nodes. They disconnect an existing "CreateGradientFromCamera" group and introduce a new "Lerp" (Linear Interpolate) node. The output from a "Near Colour" group is connected to the "A" input of the Lerp, and the output from a "Far Colour" group is connected to the "B" input. The previously detached "CreateGradientFromCamera" group's output is then connected to the "Alpha" input of the Lerp node. Finally, the output of this new Lerp node is connected to the "B" input of a Multiply node, which already has a blue input, completing the material logic. After saving the material, the scene returns to the level editor, where the landscape is initially a uniform light green. The user creates a "Material Instance" from "M_MacroDistanceBlend" named "M_Inst_MacroDistanceBlend" and applies it to the second landscape. The landscape visually updates, showing a split with two different shades of green, suggesting the blend is active but needs tuning. The user then opens the "M_Inst_MacroDistanceBlend" editor, adjusts the "Far Colour" parameter to a slightly lighter green using a color picker, and then modifies the "FarDistance" (from 0 to 1000) and "FarFadeAmount" (from 0 to 500) parameters, causing the landscape's texture to seamlessly blend between the near and far distances, creating a consistent green grass appearance across the terrain.

The video segment opens (0:00-0:10) displaying a computer screen with the Unreal Engine interface. The main viewport shows a 3D environment featuring two expansive, green, grassy landmasses or plateaus, separated by a long, dark blue, narrow valley or trench. Below the main viewport, the "Content Browser" is visible, showing two spherical material assets labeled "M_Dist_MacroDistanceBlend" (highlighted in green) and "M_MacroDistanceBlend" (a lighter, off-white texture). On the right side of the screen, the "Outliner" panel lists various scene elements like "SM_SkySphere," "VolumetricCloud," and "Landscape."
